w:r.w:t: Component Library · Screen Architecture · Animations · Code Reference

This document covers only the UI implementation — Phase 2 (Component Library) and Phase 4 (Screen Implementation) from the master plan. Every component, every screen, every animation is explained in full detail: what to build, how to build it, what props it accepts, and how it connects to live data.
Follow the sections in order. Components from Phase 2 are used directly inside the screens in Phase 4, so the component library must be complete before screen work begins.
Every component in this phase is self-contained, fully typed with TypeScript, reads styles from the design token system (never hardcoded values), and works correctly in both light and dark mode.
The Button is the most-used atom in the app. It has 6 visual variants and a consistent press animation applied to every variant.
primary — solid fill with brand color. Used for main actions like Start Mission and Confirm.
secondary — outlined border, transparent fill. Used for secondary actions.
ghost — no border, no fill. Just text. Used inside cards and lists for inline actions.
danger — solid red fill. Used for destructive actions like Delete and Emergency Stop.
icon — square or circular, icon only. Used in toolbars and map overlays.
fab — floating action button. Large circular with shadow elevation. Positioned absolutely.
All 6 variants share the same Reanimated spring press animation. When the user presses the button, it scales down to 0.96. When released, it springs back to 1.0. This gives tactile feedback.

Victory Native XL renders charts directly using React Native Skia. This means the chart draws on the UI thread using native graphics — it never goes through the JavaScript bridge. The result is that charts with 500+ data points scroll and zoom at 60fps without any jank.
Do NOT use recharts, Victory Native (original), or React Native Chart Kit. These render via the JS bridge and will cause dropped frames when displaying live sensor data.
Displays pH readings over time as a line chart. pH is the most critical sensor — it should always be visible at the top of the Analytics screen.

Data point dots: only shown for the most recent 5 points. Hidden for older points to reduce clutter.

The joystick consists of two circles: a large outer ring (240px diameter) and a small inner thumb (60px). The outer ring stays fixed. The thumb moves within it.
The thumb's centre point is constrained to stay within a 100px radius of the joystick centre. This is calculated using: if (distance > MAX_RADIUS) clamp to the edge of the circle.
Dead zone: a 20px radius around the centre is treated as neutral. This prevents micro-movements from sending commands.
Optional snap mode: the movement angle is rounded to the nearest 45 degrees (8 directions). This helps when driving in straight lines.

The joystick emits commands to the WebSocket at 20Hz (every 50ms). This is achieved using a useInterval hook inside the Control screen — not inside the gesture handler itself. The interval reads the latest thumbX and thumbY shared values and sends the command.
Do not call WebSocket send() directly inside the gesture onUpdate callback. At full joystick movement, onUpdate can fire 60 times per second, which would flood the robot. Use a 20Hz interval instead.

The robot position is shown as a custom marker. The marker has a circular background and a directional arrow that rotates to match the robot's heading. When the heading changes, the arrow rotates smoothly using interpolation rather than jumping.

As the robot moves, its GPS trail is recorded. A convex hull polygon is computed from the trail points using Turf.js. This polygon is drawn on the map as a semi-transparent fill to show the area that has been covered.

FlashList · Swipe Dismiss · Filter · Alert Detail
Alerts are grouped by date into sections: Today, Yesterday, and Earlier. FlashList supports sections via the data structure format.
Each AlertItem is wrapped in a Swipeable from react-native-gesture-handler. Swiping left reveals a red delete action. When the delete action is tapped, the row animates out using Reanimated Layout.

The Fleet screen has a toggle in the navigation header to switch between grid view (2 columns) and list view (1 column). The toggle is stored in the uiStore. The change is animated — layout transitions use Reanimated Layout animation.
Each cell is a compact RobotStatusCard showing: name, status dot, battery %, current task.
Cards have a minimum height of 120px. Battery is shown as a small horizontal bar rather than the arc gauge.
Each row is a wider card showing more info: name, status, battery bar, signal bars, last GPS position, current task.
Chevron on the right to drill into robot detail screen.
Long-pressing any robot card activates multi-select mode. A visual selection indicator appears on tapped cards. A batch command bar slides up from the bottom.
Settings are organised into sections rendered as a scrollable list of grouped rows. Each setting row has a label, an optional description, and a control (toggle, text input, or disclosure arrow).
Connection — WebSocket URL, MQTT Broker, Robot ID. Changing any field triggers automatic reconnect.
Notifications — Toggle switches for 4 alert types: Battery Low, Obstacle Detected, Sensor Failure, Mission Complete.
Display — Theme toggle (dark/light), chart refresh rate (500ms / 1s / 2s), map style preference.
Security — Biometric lock toggle, session timeout selector (15min / 30min / 1hr / Never).
About — App version, build number, a Diagnostics button that shows connection status and latency.

When the biometric lock setting is enabled, the app prompts authentication whenever the app returns to the foreground after being backgrounded for more than 30 seconds. The app does not navigate to a lock screen — instead it shows a modal overlay over whatever screen the user was on.
